chapter_theme: On the road to the lion's forest, Vijayan names the wilderness and the guards of the forest, then shows Tivittan the flowering woods, hill-fields and marutham country one by one, in a long series of landscape verses with no action.

781.reading: With the red sun beating down, the omai trees stand tall and sound like a house of mourning kin, as the elephants hide from the heat in their shade.
781.nuance: The mourning-house simile gives the dry forest a grief of its own; the grammar of the third line and the word division are rough.

782.reading: In the dry season the nelli's withered branches creak, and the sun's glare drops its shade as though fire were falling from the branches all around.
782.nuance: The lines are compressed and the first line's sense of weeping or drought is not settled; read with caution.

783.reading: The snake rages while the gloriosa climbs, and the lily flowers on the cloud-fed shoots stand like a bow-wielding deer-hunter's hand, so the rain seems about to return.
783.nuance: The picture of cloud-sent rain and gloriosa blossoms is hard to construe; the verse may turn on a simile of the flower as a hand.

784.reading: Seeing the white chariot rush past, the thirsty deer herd droops like a noble who begged from a worthless man's eyes and met blame.
784.nuance: The simile ranks begging of the base as a stain on the high-born, which the narrator accepts as common ground; the first two lines are loosely worded.

claims.claim: a noble who begs from the base earns blame

785.reading: The drummers and bowmen who do cruel deeds and eat the border land's spoil guard the forest, and none stand there but the addressee's own servants.
785.nuance: The guards are the king's own hunters, so the wild place is held by men who live by violence on his behalf.

786.reading: Naming the lands that the lion-conquering red-eyed one and the king of the white-tusked elephant hold, the moon-hued prince praises them and says these are the addressee's.
786.nuance: The epithets are heavy and the line division is rough; the identification of the moon-hued one with Vijayan comes from 778 and 800.
786.event: Vijayan, praising the country, begins to show Tivittan the lands that are his to hold.

787.reading: The land of our lord abounds in water that rises in all seasons, in the grace of the monsoon and in floods that swell in the rivers.
787.nuance: The grammar is compressed; the speaker is taken as Vijayan, 'our lord' being the king.

788.reading: The east wind dances, the bees sing, and the creeper-woman watches the play while the konrai drops gold and the gloriosa turns its hand away.
788.nuance: The whole verse is a play with the wind as dancer, the flowers as audience and the bees as singers.

789.reading: The gloriosa that opens its hand, the dark water lilies, the wide-open eyes of the flower rounds, the smiling jasmine and the curled clusters bend and bear fruit.
789.nuance: The syntax runs on into 790; the verse is a list whose verb comes in the next verse.

790.reading: Fruit that reddens like a lip, vines slim as a waist and everything seen catching the eye, so the forest looks like a garland of women.
790.nuance: The forest is likened to women, which is the poet's usual way of praising a land's loveliness.

791.reading: Jasmine spread under the moonlight, bees singing on the sandbank and the places of white sand look to one side as though the moon had spread.

792.reading: The bees circling the nectar-rich blossoms in the jambul grove make the forest look dark, as if a lump of night were sleeping there.

793.reading: The ripe tondai fruit and the thorny coral-red flowers of the thonri make the forest glow like an evening sky.

794.reading: The golden konrai, the aghil creeper and the pollen-laden blossoms make the whole country look like molten gold.
794.nuance: The images of gold and the flowers' dust are heaped on one another, a way of praising the country's wealth.

795.reading: The peacocks dance and the green crops move with the wind like a sea of water in the monsoon-glad forest.

796.reading: At the sound of the cowherds' and bards' drums the peacocks dance and the deer herds delight in the festival of the land beside the hill.
796.nuance: The festival is imagined, with the peacocks as dancers and the deer as spectators.

797.reading: The riverbank, where sand-banks, creepers and the pollen of flowers lie, looks like a sacrificial hall, and the addressee is said to wear a garland on his chest.
797.nuance: The sacrificial-hall simile (யாகசாலை) is the poem's picture of orderly beauty; it says nothing for or against the rite, and the Jain poet uses it as a plain figure.

798.reading: The cows' milk streams from udders as the calves suck, the birds feed and sing, and the jasmine opens as if to taste the flow.
798.nuance: Milk, flowers and birds are given human mouths and gestures.

799.reading: The clouds drip water on the hills, the jasmine opens in the fields, and the guests go on to the wide stretches where fish and water-birds dwell.
799.nuance: The last line shifts to the farming country, so the verse marks the travellers' passage from forest to field.

800.reading: The rain-fed nectar flows from the fresh-opened flowers into the marutham water, and the moon-bright prince tells his companion to look at this.
800.nuance: The last two lines name the speaker's glory, which makes this verse a turning point from the forest to the farm country.
800.event: Vijayan, pointing, tells Tivittan to look at the water of the farming country.

801.reading: The addressee is told to look at the fish that dart away and the young swans that rise from the shallows as the water swells, turning cloudy and bright.
801.nuance: The word division is broken; the sense of the first lines is only roughly clear.

802.reading: The jackfruit segments, the plantain's fruit and the heaps of mangoes in the orchard have become the places of the meeting of lovers and guests.
802.nuance: The sense of the last line is uncertain; 'kalavi' is taken as mingling or union.

803.reading: The monkeys eat the fruits of the mango, groan with fullness, and the male langur hides under the plantain leaf while the hill-field she-monkeys wail.
803.nuance: The picture of monkeys' wailing is played for comedy; the verse closes the series of 'look at this' verses.

links.note: Kural 1067 begs the beggars not to beg of those who conceal; verse 784 likens a deer's thirst to a high-born man who begged from a low man's eyes and earned blame.
links.teaches: The verse makes the cost of begging of the wrong person a stain on rank, where the couplet gives only a warning.

gains.a: The simile lacks the Kural's rule that the fault lies in begging of those who conceal, which names why the noble is blamed.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the sense that the shame falls harder on the high-born, which the verse's noble adds.

links.note: Kural 742 counts a shady forest as one of a fort's four parts; verse 785 shows who holds the forest, men who live by violence and serve the king.
links.teaches: A forest that guards the realm is held by violent servants, a cost the couplet's list of fort parts does not show.

gains.a: The verse lacks the idea that the forest is itself a defence, which the couplet names.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the picture of who actually keeps the forest, which the verse adds.

links.note: Akananuru 45 has the lover cross a summer forest with rattling dry pods and a tiger on the waterless track; verse 781 shows the same dry forest, with trees keening like a mourning house.
links.teaches: The same summer forest is a woman's dread in the Sangam poem and a mourning house in the epic.

gains.a: The verse lacks the human reason for the forest's dread, the parted woman, which the Akananuru poem supplies.
gains.b: The Akananuru poem lacks the image of the forest as a house of mourners, which the epic adds.

links.note: Verse 781 shows the dry forest in the heat; verse 795 shows the same wooded country green and dancing with peacocks.
links.teaches: The two verses show that the harsh forest of the first part gives way to a country of plenty as the party travels on.

links.note: Verse 786 has the moon-hued prince say 'these are yours, see them'; verse 800 repeats the 'see this' as he points to the marutham water.
links.teaches: The pointing opened at the start of the tour is carried through the whole series up to the farm country.

cast.role: the elder prince, the moon-hued one who shows the country to Tivittan, so taken from 778 and 800
the younger prince, the red-eyed dark one addressed as 'kazhaloy' (801) and 'aaramaarba' (797)

source_issues: Verses 781 to 785: the speaker is taken as Vijayan from 778, which says he spoke of the fierce forest; the verses do not name him.
Verses 781 to 789, 797, 799, 801 to 803: the word division and compressed grammar leave the sense uncertain; flagged.
Verse 786: the epithets are heavy and the line division is rough.
